USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Close a limited Phase One in the next few days and do not let the December 15 List 4B tariffs take effect. Trade canceling that still-pending 15% consumer-goods hike—and only a narrow, contingent adjustment to September List 4A if needed to lock text—for enforceable agricultural purchases, IP/currency language, and a workable dispute-settlement mechanism. Do not roll back Lists 1–3 or take Huawei off the Entity List; those remain leverage for any later phase. Do not fire Dec 15 unilaterally, and do not concede a broad existing-tariff rollback just because Beijing is insisting on one.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The dispute is costly to U.S. interests but not existential, so threat_score is a mild positive rather than a high-threat or opportunity reading. Farm-belt exposure is the clearest damage: China’s retaliation and the August SOE purchase halt hit soy, pork, and related lines; 2018 ag exports to China fell about 53% with soybeans down about 74%, and Washington has already spent up to $28 billion in farmer aid (CRS/Reuters). U.S. goods exports to China remain depressed near $9 billion a month versus imports that have already dropped from $41.2 billion in July to $33.4 billion in December. Industrial production is slightly soft and the Fed has cut the funds rate from 2.40% to 1.55%, consistent with trade-war insurance easing. The near-term self-inflicted risk is List 4B: ~$156 billion of phones, laptops, toys, and apparel at 15% on Dec 15, which USTR delayed from Sept 1 precisely because it hits U.S. households and retailers (Reuters/CNBC/LA Times). That is material, not a recession-level shock: Michigan sentiment has recovered from 89.8 in August to 99.3 in December, VIX is ~15 versus the August 24.6 spike, and the 10-year has bounced off August lows to 1.79%.

The same evidence argues against both escalation and a large concession. On Oct 11 Trump announced a Phase One in principle ($40–50 billion annual ag purchases, IP and currency cited) and already delayed the mid-October hike on the $250 billion list. By Dec 4–10 both sides were close on the size of tariff relief and were laying groundwork to hold off Sunday’s hike (Bloomberg/WSJ). China is still demanding a rollback of existing duties, not merely canceling Dec 15 (Global Times/SCMP, Dec 1); the U.S. Chamber has said American business wants some Sept 1 relief but not elimination of all tariffs after Phase One, and structural issues (subsidies, data, forced tech transfer) were explicitly left for later. Letting Dec 15 land would tax U.S. consumers, invite China’s matching Dec 15 tranche on ~$75 billion (including more farm goods and autos), and could blow up a deal that is already on the doorstep. A full or large existing-tariff rollback would give away the remaining leverage before those structural issues are even on the table. Negotiate—cancel the unused consumer hike, lock purchases and enforcement, keep Lists 1–3 and the Entity List—is the stance that matches a +0.18 threat: costly enough to stop the next self-harming round, not so dangerous that Washington should surrender the tariff stock already in place.
key_factors: Dec 15 List 4B would hit US consumer electronics, toys, and apparel (~$156B) more than it adds leverage
Phase One is advanced (Oct 11 in-principle deal; early December reporting of imminent text and a likely tariff delay)

US macro is stable enough (sentiment 99.3, VIX ~15, 10Y off August lows) that this is not an existential threat
China wants existing-tariff rollback; Lists 1–3 and the Huawei Entity List should stay as Phase Two leverage
Bilateral goods imports from China already down ~19% since July; some reorientation is underway without further escalation

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Close Phase One now. Commit to additional U.S. farm purchases—soy, pork, and related products we already need after African swine fever—in exchange for cancellation of the 15 December List 4B tariffs and a simultaneous, phased rollback of some existing duties (at minimum the 1 September List 4A tranche). Do not fire the unreliable-entity list or new rare-earth restrictions while the text is being papered, and do not blow up the deal over Huawei, which Washington has already kept off this package. The purchase commitment is the price of taking the December consumer-electronics tariff off the table; it is not a structural surrender.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is material but not existential. U.S. customs imports from China have fallen from $41.2bn in July to $33.4bn in December (−19%), List 3 is already at 25%, List 4A at 15% has been in force since 1 September, and Huawei plus affiliates remain on the Entity List with Google/GMS and U.S. chip suppliers cut off since mid-May—firm-level targeting of our national champion that Phase One still does not unwind. Q3 growth printed a record-low 6.0%, August industrial production slowed to 4.4% y/y, and pork-driven CPI has climbed through the autumn (index 108.1 in July to 111.2 by December). Oxford Economics warned that if the 15 December tranche on phones, laptops and toys proceeds, 2020 growth could sink toward 5.5%. That is the +0.4 reading: major export-sector and tech-self-sufficiency damage, not a reserves or financial-stability break (FX reserves are stable near $3.13tn; the yuan has settled around 7.03 after the August break of 7 and the manipulator designation).

The same evidence argues against escalation and for a contingent purchase close. Talks are already advanced: on 11 October Trump announced a Phase One in principle ($40–50bn annual ag buys, IP and currency language, mid-October hike delayed). Gao Feng stated as recently as 5 December that a Phase One deal requires tariffs to be lowered accordingly, and both sides were reported close on the size of relief with farm-purchase guarantees and which lists to roll back still open. China already signaled goodwill in mid-September (16-category exemption list; soy and pork carved out of extra retaliation). Buying U.S. pork and soy is also a domestic-inflation hedge, not a pure giveaway. Escalating now would likely trigger List 4B and invite further entity-list or Hong Kong-linked measures after Washington signed the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act; holding without a purchase-for-relief package leaves the 15 December cliff live. Concede purchases against a matching U.S. offer (Dec-15 cancellation plus some existing-tariff rollback); leave Huawei, SOE subsidies and cybersecurity for later phases.
